data.title: SQL
data.tagline: Ask a relational database to read or change structured records
data.description: SQL can select, filter, join, insert, update, and delete data in relational databases. Parameterize user values instead of building query strings, and inspect indexes and execution plans when a query becomes slow. A correct query still needs authorization around it.

avoid: Concatenate untrusted input into a query
Select every column when only a few are needed
Run an unbounded update or delete
Assume a database permission replaces application authorization

explanation.title: SQL vs NoSQL: which fits your data?
explanation.text: SQL is a query language; the actual choice is between a relational database and a specific NoSQL database. Compare them by data relationships, access patterns, and consistency needs—not by assuming one is faster. Data structure: Relational (SQL) — Stores structured records in tables and connects related data through fields.; NoSQL database — Uses models such as document, key-value, wide-column, or graph.. Decision point: Relational (SQL) — Often the direct fit when joins, constraints, and transactions matter.; NoSQL database — Can fit a well-defined data model and access pattern with a purpose-built product.. Typical fit: Relational (SQL) — Orders, accounts, and other related business records that need consistency.; NoSQL database — Key-value caches, documents, event records, or graph relationships.. Creating an e-commerce order: When an order connects customer, inventory, and payment records, a relational database is often the direct fit. If logs are mainly written and read by device ID at high volume, a purpose-built key-value or document database may fit better. NoSQL products differ widely, so test the specific product against the real workload.

lessonPractice.title: For a current user’s incomplete tasks, which SQL boundary is safer?

options.label: Filter by current user and incomplete status, returning only fields the page needs
options.feedback: Correct. The query limits ownership and state so it does not read unrelated or other users’ data.

options.label: Query every task and hide other users’ rows in the browser
options.feedback: The data is already sent to the client; hiding it there does not protect access.

options.label: Use SELECT * as long as incomplete status is filtered
options.feedback: Even with correct rows, do not return sensitive or unused fields without need.

data.agentPrompt: Make the task-list endpoint query only the current user’s incomplete tasks and return only fields used by the page. Test with two users’ data: each must see only their incomplete items, and the response must omit unnecessary sensitive columns.
